before.claim: For each $i$, [F1] gives a point in $\operatorname{dom}g_i$. The empty tuple is a choice for the first zero blocks; if a tuple has been constructed for the first $k<n$ blocks, append one point from the nonempty $\operatorname{dom}g_{k+1}$. Induction [F2] gives a tuple $x$ in all $n$ domains, so $g(x)<+\infty$ and $g$ is proper. Only finitely many choices are made.

If $g(x),g(y)<+\infty$ and $0\le\theta\le1$, apply the convexity inequality in [F1] to each pair $(x_i,y_i)$ and add the finitely many inequalities. If either endpoint has infinite $g$ value, the extended-real inequality is automatic under the endpoint convention. Thus $g$ is convex.

Fix a block $i$ and a real $c$. Its weak sublevel $C_{i,c}=\{u_i:g_i(u_i)\le c\}$ is closed: the map $u_i\mapsto(u_i,c)$ preserves Euclidean distances and is continuous, so $C_{i,c}$ is its preimage of the closed set $\operatorname{epi}g_i$ from [F1]. Therefore, whenever $g_i(x_i)>c$, the open complement of $C_{i,c}$ is a neighborhood of $x_i$ throughout which $g_i>c$.

Take any $(x,t)\notin\operatorname{epi}g$. If all $g_i(x_i)$ are finite, put $s=\sum_i g_i(x_i)>t$ and $c_i=g_i(x_i)-(s-t)/(2n)$. By step 1.3, each $x_i$ has an open neighborhood on which $g_i>c_i$, so their product is a neighborhood of $x$ on which $g(u)>\sum_i c_i=(s+t)/2$. With $\eta=(s-t)/4>0$, the product of these neighborhoods and $(t-\eta,t+\eta)$ misses $\operatorname{epi}g$, because its height coordinate is below $t+\eta<(s+t)/2$.

If some $g_i(x_i)=+\infty$, take the least such index $i$. For each $j
e i$, put $c_j=g_j(x_j)-1$ when that value is finite, and $c_j=0$ when it is infinite. Choose $B=t+1-\sum_{j
e i}c_j$. Since $g_i(x_i)>B$ and $g_j(x_j)>c_j$, step 1.3 supplies an open neighborhood of each block on which the corresponding strict lower bound holds. Throughout their product, $g(u)>B+\sum_{j
e i}c_j=t+1$. Restrict the epigraph-height coordinate to $(t-1/2,t+1/2)$; this neighborhood also misses $\operatorname{epi}g$.

Every point outside $\operatorname{epi}g$ is covered by one of steps 2.1 or 2.2, so its complement is open and $\operatorname{epi}g$ is closed. With $\eta=(s-t)/4>0$, the product of these neighborhoods and $(t-\eta,t+\eta)$ misses $\operatorname{epi}g$, because its height coordinate is below $t+\eta<(s+t)/2$.

If some $g_i(x_i)=+\infty$, take the least such index $i$. For each $j
e i$, put $c_j=g_j(x_j)-1$ when that value is finite, and $c_j=0$ when it is infinite. Choose $B=t+1-\sum_{j
e i}c_j$. Since $g_i(x_i)>B$ and $g_j(x_j)>c_j$, step 1.3 supplies an open neighborhood of each block on which the corresponding strict lower bound holds. Throughout their product, $g(u)>B+\sum_{j

before.quote:
Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its effective domain is $\operatorname{dom}g=\{x:g(x)<+\infty\}$. The function is **proper** if $\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing$; it is **convex** if
$$g((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)g(x)+\theta g(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ 0\le\theta\le1),$$
using the endpoint convention $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]]. It is **closed** (equivalently, lower semicontinuous in the extended-real convex-analysis convention used here) if its epigraph
$$\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:g(x)\le s\}$$
is closed in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. The proximal-gradient items on this page assume $g$ is proper, closed and convex.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

before.claim: Fix a block $i$, a point $z_i$ with $g_i(z_i)<+\infty$, and put $h=z_i-x_{B_i}$. For $0<t<1$, block minimality and convexity of $g_i$ give $0\le f(x+U_i(th))-f(x)+g_i(x_{B_i}+th)-g_i(x_{B_i})\le f(x+U_i(th))-f(x)+t[g_i(z_i)-g_i(x_{B_i})]$. Rearranging, dividing by $t>0$, and taking $t\downarrow0$ yields $g_i(z_i)-g_i(x_{B_i})\ge-\langle\nabla_i f(x),z_i-x_{B_i}\rangle$. For $g_i(z_i)=+\infty$ the same subgradient inequality is automatic. Thus $-\nabla_i f(x)\in\partial g_i(x_{B_i})$ by [F1].
For any $z=(z_{B_i})_i$, sum the block inequalities from step 1.1 to obtain $g(z)\ge g(x)-\langle\nabla f(x),z-x\rangle$. By [F1], this says $-\nabla f(x)\in\partial g(x)$.

Convex differentiability gives $f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),z-x\rangle$. Adding the inequality in step 2.1 gives $F(z)\ge F(x)$ for every $z$, so $x$ is globally minimizing and all the stated stationarity inclusions hold.

If a scalar-valued $f:U	o\mathbb R$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)=\langle
abla f(a),vangle$ for every $v$. Among unit vectors $v$, this is at most $\|
abla f(a)\|_2$; if the gradient is nonzero, equality holds exactly in the direction $
abla f(a)/\|
abla f(a)\|_2$. If the gradient is zero, every unit direction has directional derivative zero.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. Then $f$ is convex if and only if

$$f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Equivalently, $\nabla f(x)$ is a subgradient at every $x$ ([[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

before.claim: Complete the square in $q_i$: with $v_i=x_i-M_i^{-1}\nabla_i f(x)$, its $u$-dependent terms are $g_i(u)+(M_i/2)\|u-v_i\|_2^2$. Taking $t=1/M_i>0$ in [F2]–[F4] proves the exact block minimizer exists and is unique.

For an exact update, $q_i(u^*)\le q_i(x_i)=g_i(x_i)$. For an accepted inexact update, [F1] gives $q_i(u)\le q_i(u^*)+\epsilon_k\le q_i(x_i)+\epsilon_k$. before.quote: Let $F(x)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x_{B_i})$ on $\mathbb R^d$, where $B_1,\ldots,B_n$ is a disjoint nonempty block partition, $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is convex and continuously differentiable, and each $g_i:\mathbb R^{|B_i|}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper, closed and convex. Let $L_i>0$ satisfy the block-gradient Lipschitz bound of [[lem-coordinate-block-smoothness-descent-model]], choose majorizers $M_i\ge L_i$, probabilities $p_i>0$ with $\sum_i p_i=1$, a feasible initial point $x^0$, an update budget $K$, and nonnegative inner tolerances $\epsilon_0,\ldots,\epsilon_{K-1}$.

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the set $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$ is a singleton. Its unique element $u$ satisfies the resolvent equivalence
$$u=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v-u)/t\in\partial g(u).$$
For any $v_1,v_2$ and $u_i=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v_i)$,
$$\|u_1-u_2\|_2^2\le\langle u_1-u_2,v_1-v_2\rangle.$$
In particular the proximal map is nonexpansive.

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex, and let $t>0$. For $v\in\mathbb R^n$, define the set-valued proximal mapping
$$\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)=\left\{u\in\mathbb R^n:g(u)+\frac{\|u-v\|_2^2}{2t}\le g(w)+\frac{\|w-v\|_2^2}{2t}\text{ for every }w\in\mathbb R^n\right\}.$$
The existence and uniqueness theorem on this page proves that this set is a singleton for every admissible $g,t,v$; its unique member is also denoted $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$.

$$g((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)g(x)+\theta g(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ 0\le\theta\le1),$$
using the endpoint convention $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]]. It is **closed** (equivalently, lower semicontinuous in the extended-real convex-analysis convention used here) if its epigraph
$$\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:g(x)\le s\}$$
is closed in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. The proximal-gradient items on this page assume $g$ is proper, closed and convex.

Let $f:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable, let $B_i$ be one block of a finite coordinate partition, and let $U_i$ be its coordinate insertion map. Suppose $L_i>0$ satisfies $\|
abla_i f(x+U_i h)-
abla_i f(x)\|_2\le L_i\|h\|_2$ for every $x,h$. Then
$$f(x+U_i h)\le f(x)+\langle
abla_i f(x),hangle+ rac{L_i}{2}\|h\|_2^2.$$

after.quote:
Whenever a subscript $i$ indexes a block, $x_i$ is shorthand for $x_{B_i}$.

Let $F(x)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x_{B_i})$ on $\mathbb R^d$, where $B_1,\ldots,B_n$ is a disjoint nonempty partition of coordinate labels $\{1,\ldots,d\}$, with label $j$ denoting standard coordinate $j-1$. Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be convex and continuously differentiable in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], and let each $g_i:\mathbb R^{|B_i|}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex. Define $\nabla_i f(x)$ from [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] as the entries of $\nabla f(x)$ on the labels in $B_i$, in increasing order; their existence follows from total differentiability and [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Let $L_i>0$ satisfy the block-gradient Lipschitz bound of [[lem-coordinate-block-smoothness-descent-model]], choose majorizers $M_i\ge L_i$, probabilities $p_i>0$ with $\sum_i p_i=1$, a feasible initial point $x^0$, an update budget $K\in\mathbb N$, and nonnegative inner tolerances $\epsilon_0,\ldots,\epsilon_{K-1}$.

At update $k$, draw $I_k$ with probabilities $(p_i)$ independently of previous draws. For the selected block $i=I_k$, form
$$q_i^k(u)=\langle\nabla_i f(x^k),u-x^k_{B_i}\rangle+\frac{M_i}{2}\|u-x^k_{B_i}\|_2^2+g_i(u).$$
In exact mode, set $x^{k+1}_{B_i}$ to the global minimizer of $q_i^k$; leave every other block unchanged. In certified-inexact mode, an inner oracle returns $(u_k,\delta_k)$ with a certificate
$$0\le q_i^k(u_k)-\inf_u q_i^k(u)\le\delta_k\le\epsilon_k;$$
accept $u_k$ only when that certificate is available and valid. Otherwise return the last accepted point with status `inner-solve-failure`. The output is the current point, its objective value, the last certified inner gap when available, and status `tolerance-met`, `budget-limit`, or `inner-solve-failure`.

If a proximal-gradient stopping tolerance $\eta\ge0$ is requested, after each accepted update compute the block mapping
$$G_M(x)=\big(M_i[x_{B_i}-\operatorname{prox}_{g_i/M_i}(x_{B_i}-M_i^{-1}\nabla_i f(x))]\big)_{i=1}^n.$$
Here $\operatorname{prox}_{g_i/M_i}$ abbreviates $\operatorname{prox}_{(1/M_i)g_i}$, a singleton by [[def-proximal-mapping]] and [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]; $M_i>0$ by the input conditions. Stop with `tolerance-met` when $\|G_M(x)\|_2\le\eta$; otherwise stop after at most $K$ accepted updates with `budget-limit`. A finite budget or tolerance status is not an uncomputed objective-gap guarantee. Uniform sampling is $p_i=1/n$; nonuniform choices require the separate probability/step relation proved for the smooth gradient branch on this page.

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the set $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$ is a singleton. Its unique element $u$ satisfies the resolvent equivalence
$$u=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v-u)/t\in\partial g(u).$$
For any $v_1,v_2$ and $u_i=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v_i)$,
$$\|u_1-u_2\|_2^2\le\langle u_1-u_2,v_1-v_2\rangle.$$
In particular the proximal map is nonexpansive.

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex, and let $t>0$. For $v\in\mathbb R^n$, define the set-valued proximal mapping
$$\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)=\left\{u\in\mathbb R^n:g(u)+\frac{\|u-v\|_2^2}{2t}\le g(w)+\frac{\|w-v\|_2^2}{2t}\text{ for every }w\in\mathbb R^n\right\}.$$
The existence and uniqueness theorem on this page proves that this set is a singleton for every admissible $g,t,v$; its unique member is also denoted $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$.

$$g((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)g(x)+\theta g(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ 0\le\theta\le1),$$

$$\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:g(x)\le s\}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

before.claim: By [F1], $F$ is nonincreasing at every block update, so all cycle and within-cycle iterates remain in $S$. By [F4], $F$ is lower semicontinuous; it is real-valued on $S$ because $F\le F(x^0)<+\infty$. Thus [F5] bounds it below on $S$. By [F7], $L=\inf_k F(x^k)$ is real; for each $\varepsilon>0$, [F7] gives $j$ with $F(x^j)<L+\varepsilon$, and monotonicity then gives $L\le F(x^k)\le F(x^j)<L+\varepsilon$ for all $k\ge j$. Hence the full-sweep values tend to $L$.

Fix any accumulation point $\bar x$ of the full-sweep iterates and a subsequence $x^{k_j}\to\bar x$. The intermediate states $y_j^0=x^{k_j},y_j^1,\ldots,y_j^n=x^{k_j+1}$ satisfy $F(x^{k_j})\ge F(y_j^i)\ge F(x^{k_j+1})$. Both endpoint values tend to $L$, so every intermediate value tends to $L$. By [A1] and continuity of the finitely many block maps, each $y_j^i$ converges to a limit $\bar y^i$, with $\bar y^0=\bar x$.

Fix $i$. Let $a_j$ be the coordinates other than block $i$ in $y_j^{i-1}$, and let $u_j^-$ and $u_j^+$ be its block-$i$ coordinates before and after the update. Then $a_j\to\bar a$, $u_j^-\to\bar u^-$, and $u_j^+\to\bar u^+$ by step 2.1; exactness gives $u_j^+=T_i(a_j)$. Write $m_i(a)=\min_u\{f(a,u)+g_i(u)\}$. Since the other penalties cancel, the objective decrease is $d_j=f(a_j,u_j^-)+g_i(u_j^-)-m_i(a_j)$, and $d_j\to0$ because the two intermediate objective values both tend to $L$. By [F2], $m_i(a_j)\to m_i(\bar a)$; continuity of $f$ and lower semicontinuity of $g_i$ imply $f(\bar a,\bar u^-)+g_i(\bar u^-)\le m_i(\bar a)$. The reverse inequality follows from the minimum definition, so $u^-=T_i(\bar a)$ by uniqueness. Continuity of $T_i$ gives $\bar u^+=T_i(\bar a)=\bar u^-$, hence $\bar y^i=\bar y^{i-1}$.

Applying step 3.1 for $i=1,\ldots,n$ shows every within-sweep limit equals $\bar x$ and that $\bar x$ minimizes every block slice. Since $\bar x\in S$ and $F(x^0)<+\infty$, $F(\bar x)<+\infty$. By [F3], $\bar x$ satisfies the composite stationarity condition and is globally minimizing. Since $\bar x$ was arbitrary, every accumulation point is global.

The sequence lies in compact $S$, so [F6] supplies an accumulation point. If the global minimizer is unique, step 4.1 makes it the only possible accumulation point. Fix $\varepsilon>0$. If infinitely many full-sweep indices lay outside the open $\varepsilon$-ball, their increasing sequence can be chosen by taking the least next natural index each time; [F6] then gives a convergent subsequence in the closed complement, producing a different accumulation point. Thus all sufficiently late full-sweep iterates lie in the ball. For any within-sweep position, compactness of $S$ gives a convergent subsequence of those states; passing to a further subsequence, [F6] makes the cycle starts converge, and steps 2.1 and 3.1 force the within-sweep limit to equal that full-sweep accumulation point. Hence each within-sweep sequence also has only the unique minimizer as an accumulation point and converges to it by the same compact-complement argument.

after.claim: By [F1], $F$ is nonincreasing at every block update, so all cycle and within-cycle iterates remain in $S$. By [F9], $f$ is continuous, so [F4] makes $F$ lower semicontinuous; it is real-valued on $S$ because $F\le F(x^0)<+\infty$. Thus [F5] bounds it below on $S$. By [F7], $L=\inf_k F(x^k)$ is real; for each $\varepsilon>0$, [F7] gives $j$ with $F(x^j)<L+\varepsilon$, and monotonicity then gives $L\le F(x^k)\le F(x^j)<L+\varepsilon$ for all $k\ge j$. Hence the full-sweep values tend to $L$.

Fix any accumulation point $\bar x$ of the full-sweep iterates and a subsequence $x^{k_j}\to\bar x$. Since $S$ is compact, [F8] makes it closed and therefore $\bar x\in S$. The intermediate states $y_j^0=x^{k_j},y_j^1,\ldots,y_j^n=x^{k_j+1}$ satisfy $F(x^{k_j})\ge F(y_j^i)\ge F(x^{k_j+1})$. Both endpoint values tend to $L$, so every intermediate value tends to $L$. By [A1] and continuity of the finitely many block maps, each $y_j^i$ converges to a limit $\bar y^i$, with $\bar y^0=\bar x$.

Fix $i$. Let $a_j$ be the coordinates other than block $i$ in $y_j^{i-1}$, and let $u_j^-$ and $u_j^+$ be its block-$i$ coordinates before and after the update. Then $a_j\to\bar a$, $u_j^-\to\bar u^-$, and $u_j^+\to\bar u^+$ by step 2.1; exactness gives $u_j^+=T_i(a_j)$. Write $m_i(a)=\min_u\{f(a,u)+g_i(u)\}$. Since the other penalties cancel, the objective decrease is $d_j=f(a_j,u_j^-)+g_i(u_j^-)-m_i(a_j)$, and $d_j\to0$ because the two intermediate objective values both tend to $L$. By [F2], $m_i(a_j)\to m_i(\bar a)$; continuity of $f$ and lower semicontinuity of $g_i$ imply $f(\bar a,\bar u^-)+g_i(\bar u^-)\le m_i(\bar a)$. The reverse inequality follows from the minimum definition, so $u^-=T_i(\bar a)$ by uniqueness. Continuity of $T_i$ gives $\bar u^+=T_i(\bar a)=\bar u^-$, hence $\bar y^i=\bar y^{i-1}$.

Applying step 3.1 for $i=1,\ldots,n$ shows every within-sweep limit equals $\bar x$ and that $\bar x$ minimizes every block slice. Since $\bar x\in S$ and $F(x^0)<+\infty$, $F(\bar x)<+\infty$. By [F3], $\bar x$ satisfies the composite stationarity condition and is globally minimizing. Since $\bar x$ was arbitrary, every accumulation point is global.

The sequence lies in compact $S$, so [F6] supplies an accumulation point. If the global minimizer is unique, step 4.1 makes it the only possible accumulation point. Fix $\varepsilon>0$. If infinitely many full-sweep indices lay outside the open $\varepsilon$-ball about that minimizer, start with the least such index and recursively choose the least later such index; infinitude makes each candidate set nonempty, while [F10] supplies the least indices and constructs the sequence. By [F6] it has a convergent subsequence with limit in $S$, and [F11] keeps that limit outside the ball, producing a different accumulation point. Thus all sufficiently late full-sweep iterates lie in the ball. For a fixed within-sweep position, suppose a subsequence of those states converges to $y$. Its cycle-start subsequence lies in compact $S$, so [F6] supplies a further subsequence converging to some $x\in S$; steps 2.1 and 3.1 show that the corresponding within-sweep states also converge to $x$, hence $y=x$ and is a full-sweep accumulation point. Therefore every convergent subsequence of within-sweep states has the unique minimizer as its limit. If infinitely many states at that position lay outside the ball, the least-index recursion and [F6] would give a convergent subsequence whose limit remains outside by [F11], a contradiction. Hence each within-sweep sequence converges to the unique minimizer as well.

before.quote:
Let $d,n\ge1$, let $B_1,\ldots,B_n$ partition the coordinates of $\mathbb R^d$ into nonempty blocks, let $F:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]$, and let $x^0$ satisfy $F(x^0)<+\infty$. A **cyclic exact block-minimization run** with sweep budget $K\in\mathbb N$ processes blocks in the fixed order $1,\ldots,n$ for at most $K$ sweeps. At the update of block $i$, hold all other coordinates at their current values and form
$$M_i(x_{-i})=\arg\min_{u\in\mathbb R^{|B_i|}}F(x_{-i},u).$$
If $M_i(x_{-i})=\varnothing$, return the last iterate and status `block-minimum-failure`. Otherwise replace the current block by any member of $M_i(x_{-i})$. If a minimizer is nonunique, the procedure is relation-valued and every member is an admissible choice; the convergence theorem on this page assumes unique continuous block-minimizer maps. After $K$ complete sweeps, return the current iterate and status `budget-limit`. The finite budget does not certify a stationary point.

Fix a block $i$ and define $m_i(a)=\min_u\{f(a,u)+g_i(u)\}$, where $a$ denotes all other blocks, $f$ is finite and continuous, and $g_i$ is proper closed convex. Suppose the minimizer map $T_i(a)$ exists, is unique, and is continuous on the parameter set in question. Then $m_i$ is continuous there.

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable and convex, and let $g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x_{B_i})$ be proper, closed and convex, with each $g_i$ proper, closed and convex on its block. Set $F=f+g$. If $F(x)<+\infty$ and $x$ globally minimizes every block slice $u\mapsto F(x_{-i},u)$, then
$$-\nabla_i f(x)\in\partial g_i(x_{B_i})\quad(1\le i\le n),\qquad -\nabla f(x)\in\partial g(x),$$
and $x$ is a global minimizer of $F$. For an extended-real convex $h$, $p\in\partial h(a)$ means $h(z)\ge h(a)+\langle p,z-a\rangle$ for every $z$.

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and convex, and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex under the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. Then $F=f+g$ is proper, closed and convex in the same convention.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with compactness as in
[[def-metric-compactness]] and the three variants as in
[[def-metric-compactness-variants]]. Then:

1. If $(X,d)$ is compact, it is countably compact.
2. If $(X,d)$ is compact, it is limit point compact.
3. If $(X,d)$ is countably compact, it is sequentially compact.
4. If $(X,d)$ is limit point compact, it is sequentially compact.

**Every one of the four is a theorem of ZF.** Where a subsequence is extracted,
the index at each stage is the **least** admissible one, which
[[thm-well-ordering-principle]] makes canonical and [[thm-recursion]] then
assembles into a function; where finitely many indices have to be recovered from
finitely many sets, [[lem-finite-choice]] supplies them and is itself a theorem
of ZF. Nothing below appeals to countable or to dependent choice.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below. Then $S$ has a
greatest lower bound in $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-infimum]]), and it is given by

$$\inf S = -\sup(-S), \qquad \text{where } -S = \{-s : s \in S\}.$$

In particular the complete ordered field $\mathbb{R}$ has the
greatest-lower-bound property, which is therefore not an extra axiom: it is a
consequence of the least-upper-bound property.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let $\ell$ be a
lower bound of $S$ ([[def-bounded-set]]). Then

$$\ell = \inf S \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \text{for every } \varepsilon > 0 \text{ there exists } s \in S \text{ with } s < \ell + \varepsilon.$$

In words: among the lower bounds of $S$, the infimum is exactly the one that
cannot be raised by any positive amount and still bound $S$ from below.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a\in U$, then some $C,\delta>0$ satisfy $\|f(a+h)-f(a)\|_2\le C\|h\|_2$ whenever $\|h\|_2<\delta$ and $a+h\in U$. In particular $f$ is continuous at $a$.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

Let $(N,0,\sigma)$ be a Peano system ([[def-peano-system]]), in particular the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). For any set $A$, any element $a \in A$, and any function $f : A \to A$, there is a unique function $g : N \to A$ such that $g(0) = a$ and $g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n))$ for all $n \in N$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $x^*$ be the minimizer from step 1.1 and $w=(1-\alpha)x+\alpha x^*$. Convexity of $g$ gives $g(w)\le(1-\alpha)g(x)+\alpha g(x^*)$. Iterating the scalar recurrence gives $\phi_1\le q\phi_0+\epsilon_0$; if $\phi_k\le q^k\phi_0+\sum_{j<k}q^{k-1-j}\epsilon_j$, then multiplying by $q\ge0$ and adding $\epsilon_k$ proves the formula at $k+1$. Induction over $k$ establishes the displayed bound.

Let $L_i>0$ satisfy the block-gradient Lipschitz bound of [[lem-coordinate-block-smoothness-descent-model]], choose majorizers $M_i\ge L_i$, probabilities $p_i>0$ with $\sum_i p_i=1$, a feasible initial point $x^0$, an update budget $K$, and nonnegative inner tolerances $\epsilon_0,\ldots,\epsilon_{K-1}$.

If its accepted inner point has certified model gap at most $\epsilon_k$, then the new objective is at most the old objective plus $\epsilon_k$.

Let $n\ge1$ be finite, let $d_i\ge1$, and let each $g_i:\mathbb R^{d_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed, and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. On the product $\mathbb R^{d_1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb R^{d_n}$ define $g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x_i)$. Then $g$ is proper, closed, and convex. The proof below uses only finite construction and the closed epigraphs of the separate terms.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. Then there are $a\in\mathbb R^n$ and $b\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$g(x)\ge\langle a,x\rangle+b\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n).$$

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and convex, and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex under the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. Then $F=f+g$ is proper, closed and convex in the same convention.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

Whenever a subscript $i$ indexes a block, $x_i$ is shorthand for $x_{B_i}$.

Let $F(x)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x_{B_i})$ on $\mathbb R^d$, where $B_1,\ldots,B_n$ is a disjoint nonempty partition of coordinate labels $\{1,\ldots,d\}$, with label $j$ denoting standard coordinate $j-1$. Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be convex and continuously differentiable in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], and let each $g_i:\mathbb R^{|B_i|}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex. Define $\nabla_i f(x)$ from [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] as the entries of $\nabla f(x)$ on the labels in $B_i$, in increasing order; their existence follows from total differentiability and [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Let $L_i>0$ satisfy the block-gradient Lipschitz bound of [[lem-coordinate-block-smoothness-descent-model]], choose majorizers $M_i\ge L_i$, probabilities $p_i>0$ with $\sum_i p_i=1$, a feasible initial point $x^0$, an update budget $K\in\mathbb N$, and nonnegative inner tolerances $\epsilon_0,\ldots,\epsilon_{K-1}$.

At update $k$, draw $I_k$ with probabilities $(p_i)$ independently of previous draws. For the selected block $i=I_k$, form
$$q_i^k(u)=\langle\nabla_i f(x^k),u-x^k_{B_i}\rangle+\frac{M_i}{2}\|u-x^k_{B_i}\|_2^2+g_i(u).$$
In exact mode, set $x^{k+1}_{B_i}$ to the global minimizer of $q_i^k$; leave every other block unchanged. In certified-inexact mode, an inner oracle returns $(u_k,\delta_k)$ with a certificate
$$0\le q_i^k(u_k)-\inf_u q_i^k(u)\le\delta_k\le\epsilon_k;$$
accept $u_k$ only when that certificate is available and valid. Otherwise return the last accepted point with status `inner-solve-failure`. The output is the current point, its objective value, the last certified inner gap when available, and status `tolerance-met`, `budget-limit`, or `inner-solve-failure`.

If a proximal-gradient stopping tolerance $\eta\ge0$ is requested, after each accepted update compute the block mapping
$$G_M(x)=\big(M_i[x_{B_i}-\operatorname{prox}_{g_i/M_i}(x_{B_i}-M_i^{-1}\nabla_i f(x))]\big)_{i=1}^n.$$
Here $\operatorname{prox}_{g_i/M_i}$ abbreviates $\operatorname{prox}_{(1/M_i)g_i}$, a singleton by [[def-proximal-mapping]] and [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]; $M_i>0$ by the input conditions. Stop with `tolerance-met` when $\|G_M(x)\|_2\le\eta$; otherwise stop after at most $K$ accepted updates with `budget-limit`. A finite budget or tolerance status is not an uncomputed objective-gap guarantee. Uniform sampling is $p_i=1/n$; nonuniform choices require the separate probability/step relation proved for the smooth gradient branch on this page.

For the model and inputs of [[alg-randomized-coordinate-proximal-descent]], every selected exact block subproblem has a unique minimizer. If the update is exact, the objective does not increase. If its accepted inner point has certified model gap at most $\epsilon_k$, then the new objective is at most the old objective plus $\epsilon_k$.

Let $f:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable, let $B_i$ be one block of a finite coordinate partition, and let $U_i$ be its coordinate insertion map. Suppose $L_i>0$ satisfies $\|
abla_i f(x+U_i h)-
abla_i f(x)\|_2\le L_i\|h\|_2$ for every $x,h$. Then
$$f(x+U_i h)\le f(x)+\langle
abla_i f(x),hangle+ rac{L_i}{2}\|h\|_2^2.$$

Let $n\ge1$ be finite, let $d_i\ge1$, and let each $g_i:\mathbb R^{d_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed, and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. On the product $\mathbb R^{d_1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb R^{d_n}$ define $g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x_i)$. Then $g$ is proper, closed, and convex. The proof below uses only finite construction and the closed epigraphs of the separate terms.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. Then there are $a\in\mathbb R^n$ and $b\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$g(x)\ge\langle a,x\rangle+b\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n).$$

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and convex, and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex under the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. Then $F=f+g$ is proper, closed and convex in the same convention.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and compact. Every lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded below and attains a minimum. Dually, every upper semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded above and attains a maximum.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a\in U$, then some $C,\delta>0$ satisfy $\|f(a+h)-f(a)\|_2\le C\|h\|_2$ whenever $\|h\|_2<\delta$ and $a+h\in U$. In particular $f$ is continuous at $a$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

before.claim: Put $s=\theta_1+\theta_2$. The triangle inequality gives $|\theta_1|+|\theta_2|\ge|s|$, hence by [F1], $Q_y(\theta)\ge(1-s)^2+\tfrac12|s|=2(\tfrac12s^2-s+\tfrac14|s|)+1$. By [F3]--[F4], the scalar bracket is uniquely minimized at $s=S_{1/4}(1)=3/4$.

Equality in $|\theta_1|+|\theta_2|\ge|\theta_1+\theta_2|$ holds when the two coefficients have the same sign or one is zero. Since the minimizing sum is positive, every nonnegative pair summing to $3/4$ attains the lower bound from step 1.1; every minimizer must have that sum and equality, so the displayed set is exact. It contains distinct points $(3/4,0)$ and $(0,3/4)$, and both fit to $3/4$.

For $n,d\ge1$, a deterministic design $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, response $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and penalty $\tau>0$, define the Lasso objective
$$Q_y(\theta)=\frac1n\|y-X\theta\|_2^2+2\tau\|\theta\|_1.$$
Its minimizer set is $\mathcal M(y)=\operatorname{argmin}_{\theta\in\mathbb R^d}Q_y(\theta)$. The penalty is strictly positive; no full-rank condition on $X$ is imposed. The nonemptiness, compactness, and convexity of this set are proved separately; this page defines the objective and minimizer set but does not select one minimizer.

Fix integers $n,d\ge1$, a deterministic matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, a response $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and a penalty $\tau>0$. The minimizer set $\mathcal M(y)$ of [[def-lasso-estimator]] is nonempty, compact, and convex.

Let $a>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and $\tau>0$. The scalar convex function
$$q(u)=\frac a2u^2-bu+\tau|u|\qquad(u\in\mathbb R)$$
has the unique global minimizer $u^*=S_\tau(b)/a$, where $S_\tau$ is the soft-threshold map of [[def-soft-thresholding-function]]. At $b=\tau$ and $b=-\tau$, the unique minimizer is $0$.

For $\tau>0$ and $z\in\mathbb R$, define the **soft-thresholding map**
$$S_\tau(z)=\begin{cases}z-\tau,&z>\tau,\\0,&-\tau\le z\le\tau,\\z+\tau,&z<-\tau.\end{cases}$$

before.claim: Writing $s=x_1+2x_2$, we have $\nabla_1f=s$, $\nabla_2f=2s$, and their coordinate Lipschitz constants are $1$ and $4$. At $x^0$, $s=1$ and $f(x^0)=1/2$. If coordinate $1$ is sampled with common majorizer $4$, $x_1$ becomes $3/4$, so $f=\frac12(3/4)^2=9/32$; if coordinate $2$ is sampled, $x_2$ becomes $-1/2$, so $f=0$.

Uniform averaging of the two outcomes gives expected objective $(9/32+0)/2=9/64$. In cyclic minimization, the first coordinate minimizer at $x_2=0$ is $x_1=0$, and the second coordinate minimizer at $x_1=0$ is $x_2=0$; hence the sweep reaches the global minimum.

before.quote:
Let $d,n\ge1$, let $B_1,\ldots,B_n$ be a partition of $\{1,\ldots,d\}$ into nonempty blocks, and let $U_i:\mathbb R^{|B_i|}	o\mathbb R^d$ insert a block vector in coordinates $B_i$ and put zero in the other coordinates. Let $f:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R$ be convex and continuously differentiable. For each $i$, an **$L_i$ block-gradient Lipschitz bound** is a number $L_i>0$ such that
$$\|
abla_i f(x+U_i h)-
abla_i f(x)\|_2\le L_i\|h\|_2\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^d,\ h\in\mathbb R^{|B_i|}),$$
where $
abla_i f$ is the gradient restricted to block $B_i$. Choose majorizers $M_i\ge L_i$, probabilities $p_i>0$ with $\sum_i p_i=1$, an initial point $x^0$, and a finite update budget $K\in\mathbb N$.

Let $d,n\ge1$, let $B_1,\ldots,B_n$ partition the coordinates of $\mathbb R^d$ into nonempty blocks, let $F:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]$, and let $x^0$ satisfy $F(x^0)<+\infty$. A **cyclic exact block-minimization run** with sweep budget $K\in\mathbb N$ processes blocks in the fixed order $1,\ldots,n$ for at most $K$ sweeps. At the update of block $i$, hold all other coordinates at their current values and form
$$M_i(x_{-i})=\arg\min_{u\in\mathbb R^{|B_i|}}F(x_{-i},u).$$
If $M_i(x_{-i})=\varnothing$, return the last iterate and status `block-minimum-failure`. Otherwise replace the current block by any member of $M_i(x_{-i})$. If a minimizer is nonunique, the procedure is relation-valued and every member is an admissible choice; the convergence theorem on this page assumes unique continuous block-minimizer maps. After $K$ complete sweeps, return the current iterate and status `budget-limit`. The finite budget does not certify a stationary point.

Coordinate label $j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$ here denotes standard coordinate $j-1\in\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be convex and continuously differentiable in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Its gradient $\nabla f$ is the one defined by [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; total differentiability supplies its partial derivatives by [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Define $\nabla_i f(x)$ to be the entries of $\nabla f(x)$ with labels in $B_i$, in increasing order. For each $i$, an **$L_i$ block-gradient Lipschitz bound** is a number $L_i>0$ such that
$$\|\nabla_i f(x+U_i h)-\nabla_i f(x)\|_2\le L_i\|h\|_2\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^d,\ h\in\mathbb R^{|B_i|}),$$
Choose majorizers $M_i\ge L_i$, probabilities $p_i>0$ with $\sum_i p_i=1$, an initial point $x^0$, and a finite update budget $K\in\mathbb N$.

At each update $k<K$, draw $I_k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with probabilities $(p_i)$, independently of earlier draws, and set
$$x_{B_{I_k}}^{k+1}=x_{B_{I_k}}^k-\frac{1}{M_{I_k}}\nabla_{I_k} f(x^k),\qquad x_{B_j}^{k+1}=x_{B_j}^k\quad(j\ne I_k).$$
Uniform sampling means $p_i=1/n$. The exact coordinate update is the minimizer of its quadratic model. If the caller supplies a stopping predicate, it is checked after each accepted update; on the first true result the procedure returns the current iterate with status `tolerance-met`. Every finite horizon uses only a finite product distribution on index histories.

If $M_i(x_{-i})=\varnothing$, return the last iterate and status `block-minimum-failure`. Otherwise replace the current block by any member of $M_i(x_{-i})$. If a minimizer is nonunique, the procedure is relation-valued and every member is an admissible choice; the convergence theorem on this page assumes unique continuous block-minimizer maps. After $K$ complete sweeps, return the current iterate and status `budget-limit`. The finite budget does not certify a stationary point.

before.claim: With $\beta=0$, the terms depending on $\alpha$ are $\frac12\|y-a\alpha\|_2^2+\frac12\alpha^2$. Differentiating gives $(\|a\|_2^2+1)\alpha=a^Ty=2$. The coefficient $\|a\|_2^2+1=2>0$, so this strictly convex scalar quadratic has the unique minimizer $\alpha=1$.

With $\alpha=1$, the terms depending on $\beta$ are $\frac12\|y-a-b\beta\|_2^2+\beta^2$. Differentiating gives $(\|b\|_2^2+2)\beta=b^T(y-a)=2$. The coefficient $\|b\|_2^2+2=4>0$, so this strictly convex scalar quadratic has the unique minimizer $\beta=1/2$. The residual is $(1/2,1/2)$ and $J=\frac12(1/2)+\frac12+1/4=1$. At the initial point $J(0,0)=5/2$, so the exact sweep decreases the objective.

after.claim: With $\beta=0$, bilinearity [F2] expands the terms depending on $\alpha$ as $\frac12(\|a\|_2^2+1)\alpha^2-(a^Ty)\alpha$ plus a constant. Here $\|a\|_2^2+1=2$ and $a^Ty=2$, so completing the square gives $\alpha^2-2\alpha=(\alpha-1)^2-1$ plus a constant. Thus the unique global slice minimizer is $\alpha=1$.

With $\alpha=1$, bilinearity [F2] expands the terms depending on $\beta$ as $\frac12(\|b\|_2^2+2)\beta^2-b^T(y-a)\beta$ plus a constant. Here $\|b\|_2^2+2=4$ and $b^T(y-a)=2$, so completing the square gives $2\beta^2-2\beta=2(\beta-1/2)^2-1/2$ plus a constant. Thus $\beta=1/2$ is the unique global slice minimizer. The residual is $(1/2,1/2)$ and $J=\frac12(1/2)+\frac12+1/4=1$. At the initial point $J(0,0)=5/2$, so the exact sweep decreases the objective.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Fix a finite current point $x$. Convex differentiability of $f$ gives $f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),w-x\rangle\le f(w)$. Indeed, apply its convex segment inequality at $x+s(w-x)$, subtract $f(x)$, divide by $s>0$ and let $s\downarrow0$. The proposed bound at $k=0$ is $\phi_0=\phi_0$. If $\phi_j\le q_c^j\phi_0+\sum_{\ell<j}q_c^{j-1-\ell}\epsilon_\ell$, multiply by $q_c>0$ and use step 3.1 to obtain the bound at $j+1$. Whenever a subscript $i$ indexes a block, $x_i$ is shorthand for $x_{B_i}$.

Let $F(x)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x_{B_i})$ on $\mathbb R^d$, where $B_1,\ldots,B_n$ is a disjoint nonempty partition of coordinate labels $\{1,\ldots,d\}$, with label $j$ denoting standard coordinate $j-1$. Define $\nabla_i f(x)$ from [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] as the entries of $\nabla f(x)$ on the labels in $B_i$, in increasing order; their existence follows from total differentiability and [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Let $L_i>0$ satisfy the block-gradient Lipschitz bound of [[lem-coordinate-block-smoothness-descent-model]], choose majorizers $M_i\ge L_i$, probabilities $p_i>0$ with $\sum_i p_i=1$, a feasible initial point $x^0$, an update budget $K\in\mathbb N$, and nonnegative inner tolerances $\epsilon_0,\ldots,\epsilon_{K-1}$.

At update $k$, draw $I_k$ with probabilities $(p_i)$ independently of previous draws. For the selected block $i=I_k$, form
$$q_i^k(u)=\langle\nabla_i f(x^k),u-x^k_{B_i}\rangle+\frac{M_i}{2}\|u-x^k_{B_i}\|_2^2+g_i(u).$$
In exact mode, set $x^{k+1}_{B_i}$ to the global minimizer of $q_i^k$; leave every other block unchanged. In certified-inexact mode, an inner oracle returns $(u_k,\delta_k)$ with a certificate
$$0\le q_i^k(u_k)-\inf_u q_i^k(u)\le\delta_k\le\epsilon_k;$$
accept $u_k$ only when that certificate is available and valid. Otherwise return the last accepted point with status `inner-solve-failure`. The output is the current point, its objective value, the last certified inner gap when available, and status `tolerance-met`, `budget-limit`, or `inner-solve-failure`.

If a proximal-gradient stopping tolerance $\eta\ge0$ is requested, after each accepted update compute the block mapping
$$G_M(x)=\big(M_i[x_{B_i}-\operatorname{prox}_{g_i/M_i}(x_{B_i}-M_i^{-1}\nabla_i f(x))]\big)_{i=1}^n.$$
Here $\operatorname{prox}_{g_i/M_i}$ abbreviates $\operatorname{prox}_{(1/M_i)g_i}$, a singleton by [[def-proximal-mapping]] and [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]; $M_i>0$ by the input conditions. Stop with `tolerance-met` when $\|G_M(x)\|_2\le\eta$; otherwise stop after at most $K$ accepted updates with `budget-limit`. A finite budget or tolerance status is not an uncomputed objective-gap guarantee. Uniform sampling is $p_i=1/n$; nonuniform choices require the separate probability/step relation proved for the smooth gradient branch on this page.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

$$\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:g(x)\le s\}$$

This page's closed-epigraph convention is explicit: it does not silently use an equivalence between sequential lower semicontinuity and topological closedness that would require an additional choice principle in the library's generic sequential convention. In finite dimensions this is the standard closed proper convex input to proximal algorithms.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. Then $f$ is convex if and only if

$$f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Equivalently, $\nabla f(x)$ is a subgradient at every $x$ ([[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a\in U$, then some $C,\delta>0$ satisfy $\|f(a+h)-f(a)\|_2\le C\|h\|_2$ whenever $\|h\|_2<\delta$ and $a+h\in U$. In particular $f$ is continuous at $a$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

field_operations.after:
Let $k\ge1$, $d\ge1$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be the right-hand side of a first-order initial-value problem on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$, using the convention of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **constant-step $k$-step linear multistep method** has real coefficients $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_k,\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_k$ with $\alpha_k\ne0$ and advances values by

$$\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_jY_{n+j}=h\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_j f(t_{n+j},Y_{n+j}),\qquad t_{n+j}=t_n+jh,\quad h>0.$$

Multiplying all coefficients by the same nonzero scalar leaves the method unchanged; one may normalize $\alpha_k=1$. Its **characteristic polynomials** are

$$\rho(\zeta)=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_j\zeta^j,\qquad \sigma(\zeta)=\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_j\zeta^j.$$

For an exact solution $y$ with $p+1$ continuous derivatives, the **unscaled local residual** at $t_n$ is

$$\tau_n(h;y)=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_jy(t_n+jh)-h\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_jy'(t_n+jh).$$

The method has **order at least $p$**, where $p\ge1$ is an integer, if this residual is $O(h^{p+1})$ uniformly for admitted starting times in every fixed compact interval on which the indicated derivatives are bounded. It is **consistent** if it has order at least one. Equivalently, with the above coefficient convention, consistency is $\rho(1)=0$ and $\rho'(1)=\sigma(1)$.

The **root condition** is that every complex root of $\rho$ has modulus at most one and every root of modulus one has algebraic multiplicity one. The method is **zero-stable** if for each $T>0$ there is a constant $M_T$ independent of $N$ such that every solution of the homogeneous recurrence $\sum_j\alpha_jY_{n+j}=0$ on the uniform grid $h=T/N$ satisfies

$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|Y_n\|_\infty\le M_T\max_{0\le j<k}\|Y_j\|_\infty.$$

Here $\|x\|_\infty=\max_{1\le i\le d}|x_i|$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The root-condition equivalence for zero-stability is established separately.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$

$$A\text{ is invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\det(A)\ne0.$$

$$

Fix a disk, $z\in D_j$, and $A\in\mathcal A$. The exact identity
$$

$$
and [F2] give
$$
\|I-R_j(zI-A)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}
\le e_j+s_j(|z-z_j|+\|A-A_0\|_{\infty,\mathbb C})
\le q_j<1.
$$
[F1] applies to $M=R_j(zI-A)=I-E$ with $E=I-M$, giving $\|M^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le(1-q_j)^{-1}$. Here [F4] gives $\|(z-z_j)I\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}=|z-z_j|$, and the row-sum norm's triangle inequality and compatibility [F2, F4] justify the defect estimate.

The witness $S$ establishes that $R$ is nonsingular. No independence assumption on the actual family is required beyond its inclusion in the input boxes.

1. Outward-evaluate, over the full family boxes and $x\in X$, the Krawczyk expression
$$
K=x_0-R(Ax_0-b)+(I-RA)(X-x_0).
$$
If any interval operation is not finite and defined, return `inconclusive`.

2. Compare the resulting enclosing rectangle box with $X$ by exact endpoint comparisons. If it is not contained in $X$, return `inconclusive`. Otherwise outward-bound the maximum row sum of $|I-RA|$ uniformly over the family by a number $q$. Return `existence-certified`; attach `unique-certified` for each fixed pair if $q<1$, and otherwise attach `uniqueness-inconclusive`.

The enclosure in step 1 may be wider than the exact set of Krawczyk values; only successful inclusion produces a claim. A failed inclusion or a failed norm bound does not imply singularity.

Input $n\ge1$, a nonempty family of Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices enclosed by complex rectangles, a point matrix $V\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, a real diagonal matrix $\Theta\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, and proposed nonnegative bounds $\delta,\rho,M_A,M_\Theta,\tau$. Treat point data as exact dyadics and the family as any subset of its enclosure.

1. With outward interval evaluation, enclose $V^*V-I$ and every $AV-V\Theta$ for the full family. Form Frobenius upper bounds $d,r$ for these two matrices. Also form Frobenius upper bounds $m_A$ for every $A$ in the family and $m_\Theta$ for $\Theta$. If any enclosure or square-root operation is non-finite, return `inconclusive`.

2. Verify by outward scalar comparisons that $d\le\delta<1$, $r\le\rho$, $m_A\le M_A$, $m_\Theta\le M_\Theta$, and that $1-\sqrt{1-\delta}\le\tau$. If any comparison is undecided or false, return `inconclusive` with the failed check. Otherwise set $\eta=\rho+(M_A+M_\Theta)\tau$ by outward arithmetic and return `certified` with the intervals $[\theta_{(k)}-\eta,\theta_{(k)}+\eta]$, sorted increasingly by the diagonal entries of $\Theta$.

The checks use the Frobenius norm as an upper bound for the operator 2-norm. An inconclusive check makes no statement about the true spectrum.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a nonempty family of Hermitian matrices in $\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $V\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, and let $\Theta=\operatorname{diag}(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)$ with real $\theta_j$. A **residual and orthogonality certificate** is a tuple of nonnegative numbers $\delta,\rho,M_A,M_\Theta,\tau$ such that, for every $A\in\mathcal A$,
$$\|V^*V-I\|_2\le\delta<1,\quad \|AV-V\Theta\|_2\le\rho,\quad \|A\|_2\le M_A,\quad \|\Theta\|_2\le M_\Theta,\quad 1-\sqrt{1-\delta}\le\tau.$$
The certificate uses exact inequalities or separately verified upper bounds. Its eigenvalue enclosure radius is $\eta=\rho+(M_A+M_\Theta)\tau$. This definition does not assert that computed residuals or Gram matrices satisfy the bounds; that is a separate certification procedure.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $(V,\Theta,\delta,\rho,M_A,M_\Theta,\tau)$ be a residual and orthogonality certificate for a nonempty family $\mathcal A$ of Hermitian matrices in $\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. Sort the diagonal entries of $\Theta$ increasingly as $\theta_{(1)}\le\cdots\le\theta_{(n)}$. Then every $A\in\mathcal A$ has ordered eigenvalues $\lambda_1(A)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(A)$ satisfying
$$
|\lambda_k(A)-\theta_{(k)}|\le \rho+(M_A+M_\Theta)\tau,\qquad 1\le k\le n.
$$

let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

where [F2] makes each reported upper bound outward and $\|R\|_2\le\|R\|_F$.

   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
